blocks.heading: Pseudonymous is not anonymous
text: Teodora put one address on the label's website so listeners could pay for records directly.
It was up for four days. It is now attached to every payment she will ever make.

blocks.heading: Start from what is published
text: Every transaction, amount and address, since January 2009, downloadable by anyone, permanently.
There is no login and no rate limit. The question was never whether the data is available - it is what can be inferred from it.

blocks.heading: The first guess
text: If one transaction spends three outputs, whoever made it had to sign for all three.
So all three belong to the same person. That single assumption, applied across the whole chain, merges millions of addresses into clusters.

blocks.alt: Three inputs marked as one owner feeding a transaction with two outputs, the odd-amount one marked as change
blocks.caption: One output is a payment; the other is change coming home. The amounts usually say which.

blocks.heading: Neither is certain, and it does not matter
text: A wallet can deliberately spend from unrelated coins. Change can be made to look like a payment.
But they are right often enough, and there are billions of transactions to be right about. Clusters converge.

blocks.question: Clustering only produces anonymous groups of addresses. Where does a name come from?
answer: From one point of contact with the ordinary world, and one is enough. An exchange deposit made with identity documents. An invoice paid to a known supplier. An address published on a record label's website.
The cluster was already built. The name colours all of it at once, including everything the cluster did before the link existed.

blocks.title: It works backwards in time
text: An analysis technique invented in 2032 applies to a payment made in 2026. The data cannot be withdrawn, corrected, or expired.
This is the only surveillance dataset that is complete, permanent, retroactive, and free to query.

blocks.heading: It was documented from the beginning
text: Section 10 of the whitepaper asks for **a new key pair for every transaction**, and states plainly that multi-input transactions reveal common ownership.
The privacy model was published as fragile. What drifted was the practice: one address, reused, printed on a website.

blocks.heading: What Teodora actually leaked
text: Not the record sales. The escrow to Ines, the pressing plant, her rent - anything paid from those coins joins a cluster the website already labelled with her name.
Her supplier list and roughly her turnover are now public, to anyone who cared to look.

blocks.heading: What helps, honestly
text: A fresh address per payment: free, automatic since BIP-32, and by far the largest single improvement.
CoinJoin makes the common-input assumption actually false. Taproot makes complex spends look like ordinary ones, so the script type stops being a fingerprint.
None of it touches what is already published. Privacy here is a property of decisions made before the payment, not after.
Cash is anonymous and forgets. This is pseudonymous and remembers everything.

blocks.heading: One sentence worth keeping
text: An address is not a name until it is, and when it becomes one it does so retroactively, for everything it ever touched.
Next: the twelve words that stand between Teodora and losing all of it at once.
